w: These notes come from Dr. Geurs' slides, posted before the lecture, plus the class exam-review guide. His two goals for the session: picking the right cases for regeneration, and what regeneration can actually achieve. What regeneration means Periodontal regeneration means growing back all three parts of the tooth's attachment: new bone, new cementum (the thin layer on the root) and new periodontal ligament (the fibers that hold the tooth in the bone), so the tooth has a working attachment again, on a root that gum disease had stripped bare. All three have to grow back; more bone on an X-ray isn't enough. The opposite is repair: healing that closes the wound but doesn't rebuild the original structure. After a flap or a deep cleaning, the root usually just repairs: a long strip of gum lining, a long junctional epithelium, sticks to the root instead of new cementum and fibers. What it takes Four things have to come together: cells that can build the tissue (from the ligament and bone next to the hole), a scaffold for them to grow into, growth factors that call them in and make them multiply, and a blood supply to feed it all. The slides' map splits the approaches in two. Tissue engineering brings in cells: grown in a lab, clumped together, or seeded onto a scaffold, which can even be 3D printed. Endogenous regeneration adds no cells: it calls the patient's own cells to the spot (cell homing) with growth signals, tissue matrix, tiny cell-made packages called exosomes, or drugs. Everything in this deck's cases is the second kind: grafts, membranes and biologic gels that work with the patient's own cells. Picking the case: the shape of the defect Bone holes beside the root (intrabony defects) are sorted by how many bone walls are left around them, how wide they are and how deep they are. One hole often mixes types: three walls at the bottom and fewer near the top. The best ones for regeneration are deeper than 3 mm, with walls at an angle of 25 degrees or less to the root on the X-ray, so narrow rather than wide and shallow. A 2021 review agrees: deeper, narrower defects with more walls gain more attachment and more bone a year after surgery. For example, a 1-wall hole gained about 1.2 mm less bone than a 3-wall hole, and depth was the most reliable predictor. Walls hold the blood clot and graft in place, bring in cells and blood vessels from more sides, and hold up the gum. The exam-review guide says it simply: 3-wall defects are the best candidates. A defect with mostly one wall is called non-supportive, and it's a big risk for failure. In one 2012 study, a 1-wall defect and thin, scalloped gums were the two things that predicted more gum recession on the front of the tooth after surgery. An X-ray is a flat picture of a 3-D hole; the slides' X-rays of 3-, 2- and 1-wall holes on the same skull molar look surprisingly alike. So you only really count the walls during surgery, once the gum is lifted and the hole is cleaned out. The risk checklist and the decision tree A 2023 risk checklist rates each case low, medium or high risk in four areas. The patient: healthy healing or not; smoking (none is low, 10 a day or fewer is medium, more than 10 is high); plaque left on the teeth (15% or less is low, 16 to 24% medium, 25% or more high); showing up for maintenance; and realistic hopes. The tooth: its overall gum risk; whether bite trauma and looseness can be controlled; the nerve (a healthy nerve with the hole not reaching the root tip, or a good root canal, is low; an existing root canal needs a careful look; a hole reaching the root tip, a poor root canal or a dead nerve is high); the root surface (flat is low, dented medium, two fused roots high); healthy gum or not; and gum thickness (thick is low, thin with at least 2 mm of firm gum medium, thin with little or none high). The defect: 3-wall, narrow and deep is low, 2-wall medium, 1-wall, wide and shallow high; no furcation is low, Class I or II medium, Class III high; it must be reachable to clean during surgery (front teeth easiest); and a contained hole, touching 1 or 2 sides of the root, is low, while one touching 3 or more sides is high. The surgeon: experience, stress, and whether they use a checklist. A decision tree from the AAP Regeneration Workshop says what to do. First, fix the patient: uncontrolled medical problems, smoking and other habits, and poor cleaning at home. Then, after the first round of treatment, check the pockets, bleeding, looseness, the bone and any other dental work. A bone hole under 3 mm isn't a regeneration case: pockets of 5 mm or less without bleeding get non-surgical care; deeper pockets get bone-reshaping surgery. For a hole 3 mm or deeper, the best odds go 3-wall, then circumferential or 2-wall, then 1-wall, and narrow beats wide. If the tooth's outlook is poor, it comes out and gets replaced. Otherwise the hole decides the treatment: a narrow 3-wall or circumferential hole (under 2 mm wide) gets a bone graft, a membrane or a biologic; a wide one (3 mm or more) or a 2-wall hole gets a reinforced membrane, a graft plus a membrane, or a graft plus a biologic; a 1-wall hole gets combination therapy or a bone graft that contains living cells. Looks matter too: if the patient shows a lot of gum when smiling, has thin gums or has lost the gum between the teeth, go ahead only if they accept the risk to looks, skip the membrane, and think about a gum graft. The toolbox Regeneration aims to regrow bone, cementum and ligament and gain attachment, mainly in 2- and 3-wall bone holes. The slides list bone grafts, guided tissue regeneration (GTR), combination therapy, biologics such as enamel matrix proteins or PDGF, and MIST, a minimally invasive surgery done through a small flap that keeps the gum between the teeth. Regeneration rebuilds lost support; resective surgery from Session 5 does the opposite and reshapes the bone to get rid of the pocket. Bone grafts. The slides' graft case used DFDBA (demineralized freeze-dried bone allograft): donor bone from a tissue bank. The hole was filled, and after healing the pocket measured 3 mm. Grafts are named by where they come from: autograft, from the patient; allograft, from another person; xenograft, from an animal, such as cow bone; and alloplast, a man-made material such as beta-tricalcium phosphate. Guided tissue regeneration. A thin barrier membrane goes over the hole, under the gum. Gum tissue grows much faster than bone and ligament, so the membrane keeps it off the root and gives the slower ligament and bone cells time to fill in. In combination therapy, a bone graft goes under the membrane to hold the space open so the membrane can't sag into the hole. The slides follow these cases on X-rays at 1 year, 20 years and 25 years, and the new bone was still there decades later. Biologics. Enamel matrix derivative (EMD) is a gel made from the proteins that build enamel and the tooth's attachment while the tooth develops, mostly amelogenins. Alone or with a graft, it works about as well as GTR; the slides show a case healing with it from 2022 to 2025. rhPDGF-BB is a lab-made growth factor that calls in bone and ligament cells, makes them multiply and helps new blood vessels grow. A beta-TCP scaffold is a bone-friendly framework that keeps the gum from collapsing into the hole and holds the clot steady; the exam-review guide pairs it with rhPDGF-BB. Defects without walls. When a defect has no walls to contain it, nothing holds up the gum or the clot, so a biologic gel alone has no space to work in. These defects usually get a graft too, to support the gum, which is why the decision tree sends a 1-wall hole to combination therapy. The slides follow one such case from the first X-ray through surgery, grafting and stitches to the follow-up X-ray. What can you achieve? The starting point is open flap debridement: lifting the gum and cleaning the root, with no graft. In the studies on the slide, pockets of about 7 mm came down to about 4 mm, with about 1.5 mm of attachment gained and about 1 mm of bone. The pocket shrank by 3 mm but the attachment improved by only 1.5 mm, because the rest is the gum shrinking down the root (recession). Regenerative treatments are judged by how much better they do than this. The slides show four mixes healing on X-rays over 3 to 16 months: Emdogain with donor bone, a membrane with the patient's own bone, rhPDGF with donor bone, and donor bone alone. Proving it worked There are three ways to check: histology (looking at the tissue under a microscope), clinical measurements (probing) and X-rays. Only histology can show new cementum, new ligament fibers and new bone, so only histology proves real regeneration. A probe can't tell new attachment from a long strip of gum lining stuck to the root, and an X-ray shows bone, not attachment. Subtraction radiography lines up two matching X-rays taken at different times and subtracts one from the other, so only the change shows. Dr. Geurs and colleagues used it in 1996 to test a membrane that dissolves on its own: the new bone lit up on the subtraction image, and under the microscope, 6 months later, new cementum, ligament and bone had grown into a small marker notch cut in the root.
